claim: Sclerostin downregulation in osteocytes mediates bone formation in response to mechanical cues and parathyroid hormone (PTH).
source: The downregulation of sclerostin in osteocytes mediates bone formation in response to mechanical cues and parathyroid hormone (PTH).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational claim and is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Regulation of sclerostin has been attributed exclusively to transcriptional downregulation of the Sost gene hours after stimulation.
source: To date, the regulation of sclerostin has been attributed exclusively to the transcriptional downregulation of the Sost gene hours after stimulation.
evidence: This claim is presented as established knowledge in the field, setting up the novelty of the current findings.

claim: Sclerostin protein undergoes rapid, minute-scale post-translational degradation by the lysosome following mechanical load and PTH.
source: Using mouse models and rodent cell lines, we describe the rapid, minute-scale post-translational degradation of sclerostin protein by the lysosome following mechanical load and PTH.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript supported by multiple experimental approaches including western blots and immunofluorescence.

claim: Transient inhibition of lysosomal degradation impairs load-induced bone formation by preventing sclerostin degradation.
source: Using a mouse forelimb mechanical loading model, we find transient inhibition of lysosomal degradation or the upstream mechano-signaling pathway controlling sclerostin abundance impairs subsequent load-induced bone formation by preventing sclerostin degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experiments using bafilomycin A1 to inhibit lysosomal function during mechanical loading.

claim: Transient inhibition of the upstream mechano-signaling pathway controlling sclerostin abundance impairs load-induced bone formation.
source: Using a mouse forelimb mechanical loading model, we find transient inhibition of lysosomal degradation or the upstream mechano-signaling pathway controlling sclerostin abundance impairs subsequent load-induced bone formation by preventing sclerostin degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experiments using apocynin to inhibit NOX2.

claim: Dysfunctional lysosomes in Gaucher disease lead to aberrant sclerostin regulation.
source: We also link dysfunctional lysosomes to aberrant sclerostin regulation using human Gaucher disease iPSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments showing increased sclerostin levels in Gaucher disease iPSC-derived osteoblasts.

claim: Sclerostin is a secreted 27 kDa glycoprotein that inhibits the differentiation and activity of bone-forming osteoblasts by antagonizing the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway.
source: Sclerostin (gene name Sost) is a secreted 27 kDa glycoprotein that inhibits the differentiation and activity of bone-forming osteoblasts by antagonizing the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway (Baron and Gori, 2018; Drake and Khosla, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Genetic deletion of the Sost gene in mice results in extraordinarily high bone mass.
source: Genetic deletion of the Sost gene in mice results in extraordinarily high bone mass (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Mutations in the SOST gene underlie high bone mass and bone overgrowth in patients with sclerosteosis and van Buchem disease.
source: In humans, mutations in the SOST gene underlie high bone mass and bone overgrowth in patients with sclerosteosis and van Buchem disease (Balemans et al., 2002; Balemans et al., 2001; Appelman-Dijkstra et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous clinical research.

claim: Romosozumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody targeting sclerostin, has been FDA approved to treat osteoporosis in post-menopausal women at high risk for fracture.
source: Indeed, targeting sclerostin protein with neutralizing antibodies is incredibly effective at increasing bone mass, and Romosozumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody targeting sclerostin, has been FDA approved to treat osteoporosis in post-menopausal women at a high risk for fracture (McClung, 2017; Bandeira et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Osteocytes sense and respond to fluid shear stress (FSS) in the lacunar canalicular network by decreasing sclerostin protein abundance.
source: In response to bone mechanical loading, osteocytes sense and respond to fluid shear stress (FSS) in the lacunar canalicular network by ultimately decreasing sclerostin protein abundance, de-repressing Wnt/β-catenin signaling, and unleashing osteoblast differentiation and bone formation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Intermittent administration of parathyroid hormone (PTH) causes net bone formation in part by decreasing sclerostin.
source: When administered intermittently, parathyroid hormone (PTH) causes net bone formation in part by decreasing sclerostin (Keller and Kneissel, 2005; Bellido et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Transcriptional downregulation of the Sost gene occurs on an hour timescale after mechanical load or PTH exposure.
source: To date, the regulation of sclerostin protein abundance has been attributed to the transcriptional downregulation of the Sost gene that occurs on an hour timescale after mechanical load or PTH exposure (Sebastian and Loots, 2017; Wein, 2018; Bonnet et al., 2012; Bonnet et al., 2009; Meakin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ocy454 cells are one of the few cell lines that reliably express detectable sclerostin protein.
source: Using a recently established osteocyte-like cell line, Ocy454 cells, which is one of the few cell lines that reliably express detectable sclerostin protein (Wein et al., 2015; Spatz et al., 2015), we previously described a mechano-transduction pathway that regulates osteocyte sclerostin protein abundance in response to FSS in vitro (Figure 1A; Lyons et al., 2017; Williams et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Osteocyte mechano-signaling requires a subset of detyrosinated microtubules, which transduce load signals to activate NADPH oxidase 2 (NOX2).
source: Using this in vitro model, we found that osteocyte mechano-signaling required a subset of detyrosinated microtubules, which transduce load signals to activate NADPH oxidase 2 (NOX2), which produces reactive oxygen species (ROS) signals.
evidence: This claim is based on previous work by the authors cited in the manuscript.

claim: NOX2 produces reactive oxygen species (ROS) signals in response to mechanical load.
source: Using this in vitro model, we found that osteocyte mechano-signaling required a subset of detyrosinated microtubules, which transduce load signals to activate NADPH oxidase 2 (NOX2), which produces reactive oxygen species (ROS) signals.
evidence: This claim is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: ROS signals elicit a transient receptor potential vanilloid 4 (TRPV4)-dependent primary calcium (Ca2+) influx.
source: These ROS signals then elicit a transient receptor potential vanilloid 4 (TRPV4)-dependent primary calcium (Ca2+) influx.
evidence: This claim is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: Calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase II (CaMKII) is activated in response to primary Ca2+ influx and is required for reduction of osteocyte sclerostin protein abundance.
source: Calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase II (CaMKII) is activated in response to this primary Ca2+ influx and is required for reduction of osteocyte sclerostin protein abundance (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on previous work by the authors and is supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: The loss of sclerostin protein following FSS is surprisingly rapid (minute scale) and likely distinct from transcriptional regulation of the Sost gene.
source: While these discoveries integrated with and extended several established models of the osteocyte mechanical response (Thompson et al., 2012; Schaffler et al., 2014; Geoghegan et al., 2019; Baik et al., 2013), we found the loss of sclerostin protein was surprisingly rapid (minute scale) and was likely wholly distinct from the well-characterized transcriptional regulation of the Sost gene, which occurs on the hour timescale (Sebastian and Loots, 2017; Wein, 2018; Bonnet et al., 2012; Bonnet et al., 2009; Meakin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing rapid protein loss and citations to previous work on transcriptional regulation.

claim: Sclerostin protein abundance was rapidly reduced and CaMKII activated in loaded versus contralateral non-loaded limbs within 5 minutes of ulnar loading.
source: As occurred in vitro, sclerostin protein abundance was rapidly reduced and CaMKII activated in loaded versus contralateral non-loaded limbs (Figure 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The percent of sclerostin positive osteocytes was decreased in loaded limbs versus contralateral non-loaded limbs.
source: and the percent of sclerostin positive osteocytes was decreased in loaded limbs versus contralateral non-loaded limbs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Sclerostin protein decreases as early as 1 min post-FSS in Ocy454 cells, with the nadir at 10 min, followed by a rebound.
source: A temporal assessment of sclerostin protein abundance following FSS in Ocy454 cells (Figure 1E) and UMR106 cells (Figure 1F) revealed a decrease in sclerostin protein as early as 1 min post-FSS, with the nadir of protein expression occurring at 10 min, followed by a subsequent rebound.
evidence: This claim is supported by time course western blot data shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: A single 5 min bout of FSS does not decrease Sost mRNA levels despite a decrease in sclerostin protein.
source: Consistent with the possibility of post-translational control of sclerostin, we recently reported that a single 5 min bout of FSS, as used here, does not decrease Sost mRNA levels despite a decrease in sclerostin protein (Williams et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Overexpressed sclerostin protein (myc- or GFP-tagged) under CMV promoter control was rapidly and transiently decreased by FSS.
source: Like endogenous sclerostin, overexpressed sclerostin protein was rapidly and transiently decreased by FSS (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pro-collagen type 1α1 abundance was unchanged following FSS in Ocy454 cells.
source: The regulated degradation did not extend to all proteins as pro-collagen type 1α1 abundance was unchanged following FSS in Ocy454 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), supporting some level of specificity for the regulated degradation of sclerostin.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Sclerostin protein abundance decreased after 30 min of PTH treatment in Ocy454 cells.
source: In Ocy454 cells, sclerostin protein abundance decreased after 30 min of PTH treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: PTH treatment caused sclerostin loss over a 30 min time period in GFP-sclerostin transfected Ocy454 cells.
source: Examining the post-translational regulation of sclerostin protein abundance in GFP-sclerostin transfected Ocy454 cells, we show PTH treatment caused sclerostin loss over a 30 min time period (Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: PTH treatment for 30 min does not change Sost mRNA levels.
source: with no change in Sost mRNA levels after this 30 min treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: PTH treatment of dissected tibiae ex vivo decreased sclerostin protein abundance on a minute-scale timeframe.
source: To confirm that rapid regulation occurs in an intact bone with endogenous sclerostin, dissected tibiae were treated with PTH ex vivo, which decreased sclerostin protein abundance in the same minute-scale timeframe (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PTH exposure increased phospho-CaMKII abundance in Ocy454 cells.
source: As with FSS (Lyons et al., 2017; Williams et al., 2020), PTH exposure increased phospho-CaMKII abundance (Figure 2C)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Inhibition of lysosomal function with bafilomycin A1 prevented both FSS- and PTH-induced degradation of sclerostin protein in Ocy454 cells transfected with GFP-sclerostin.
source: In Ocy454 cells transfected with GFP-sclerostin, inhibition of lysosomal function with bafilomycin A1 prevented both FSS- and PTH-induced degradation of sclerostin protein (Figure 3A,B)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Inhibition of proteasomal degradation with MG-132 had no effect on FSS-induced decrease in sclerostin.
source: whereas inhibition of proteasomal degradation with MG-132 or secretion with brefeldin A had no effect on the FSS-induced decrease in sclerostin (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Inhibition of secretion with brefeldin A had no effect on FSS-induced decrease in sclerostin.
source: whereas inhibition of proteasomal degradation with MG-132 or secretion with brefeldin A had no effect on the FSS-induced decrease in sclerostin (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Inhibition of lysosomal activity with bafilomycin A1 or leupeptin prevented FSS-induced sclerostin degradation in UMR106 osteosarcoma cells.
source: Likewise, inhibition of lysosomal activity with bafilomycin A1 or leupeptin prevented FSS-induced sclerostin degradation in UMR106 osteosarcoma cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the absence of a stimulus, the half-life of sclerostin protein is about 3 hr.
source: Notably, in the absence of a stimulus, the half-life of sclerostin protein is about 3 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by degradation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Sclerostin protein contains at least two putative sites for N-linked glycosylation (Asn-X-Ser/Thr) that are conserved across species.
source: In silico analysis of the sclerostin protein amino acid sequence identified at least two putative sites for N-linked glycosylation (Asn-X-Ser/Thr) and three Tyr-X-X-Φ lysosome targeting motifs that are conserved across species (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Sclerostin protein contains three Tyr-X-X-Φ lysosome targeting motifs that are conserved across species.
source: In silico analysis of the sclerostin protein amino acid sequence identified at least two putative sites for N-linked glycosylation (Asn-X-Ser/Thr) and three Tyr-X-X-Φ lysosome targeting motifs that are conserved across species (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both endogenous and exogenous sclerostin are found in distinct puncta in Ocy454 cells.
source: Both endogenous and exogenous sclerostin were found in distinct puncta in Ocy454 cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4A.

claim: GFP-sclerostin co-localizes with acidic vesicles identified by LysoTracker in live Ocy454 cells.
source: In live Ocy454 cells, GFP-sclerostin was co-localized with acidic vesicles identified by LysoTracker and co-localized with lysosomes labeled by siR-lysosome (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by live cell imaging shown in Figure 4B.

claim: GFP-sclerostin co-localizes with lysosomes labeled by siR-lysosome in live Ocy454 cells.
source: In live Ocy454 cells, GFP-sclerostin was co-localized with acidic vesicles identified by LysoTracker and co-localized with lysosomes labeled by siR-lysosome (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by live cell imaging shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Endogenous sclerostin co-localizes with p62/sequestosome-1 protein in fixed Ocy454 cells.
source: In fixed cells, endogenous sclerostin co-localized with p62/sequestosome-1 protein, an autophagy cargo adapter protein that shuttles proteins for lysosomal degradation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Sclerostin is found in extracellular vesicles positive for the lysosome-associated protein LAMP1.
source: That sclerostin is found localized with lysosomal adapter proteins and is degraded by the lysosome is consistent with the recent finding that sclerostin is found in extracellular vesicles positive for the lysosome-associated protein LAMP1 (Morrell et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Sclerostin co-localizes with Rab27a in Ocy454 cells.
source: Interestingly, sclerostin was also co-detected with Rab27a in Ocy454 cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Rab27a is a small GTPase that is a master regulator of the trafficking, docking, and fusion of secretory vesicles.
source: Rab27a is a small GTPase that is a master regulator of the trafficking, docking, and fusion of secretory vesicles, directs vesicles to lysosomes, and controls secretory granules in insulin-secreting beta-cells (Waselle et al., 2003; Fukuda, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The Rab27a secretory pathway regulates RANKL secretion in osteoblasts.
source: This lysosome-associated Rab27a secretory pathway also regulates RANKL secretion in osteoblasts (Kariya et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: FSS increased p62/sequestosome-1 protein abundance in Ocy454 cells.
source: Both FSS and exposure to PTH increased p62/sequestosome-1 protein abundance and increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, consistent with enhanced lysosomal delivery of autophagy cargo (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: FSS increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio in Ocy454 cells.
source: Both FSS and exposure to PTH increased p62/sequestosome-1 protein abundance and increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, consistent with enhanced lysosomal delivery of autophagy cargo (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PTH exposure increased p62/sequestosome-1 protein abundance in Ocy454 cells.
source: Both FSS and exposure to PTH increased p62/sequestosome-1 protein abundance and increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, consistent with enhanced lysosomal delivery of autophagy cargo (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: PTH exposure increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio in Ocy454 cells.
source: Both FSS and exposure to PTH increased p62/sequestosome-1 protein abundance and increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, consistent with enhanced lysosomal delivery of autophagy cargo (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: FSS induced an increase in lysosome activity as determined using Magic Red Cathepsin B activity assay.
source: Similarly, FSS induced an increase in lysosome activity, as determined using Magic Red Cathepsin B activity assay (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Magic Red assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: CaMKII activation regulates lysosomal activity and protein degradation in other tissues.
source: CaMKII activation regulates lysosomal activity and protein degradation in other tissues (Reventun et al., 2017; Li et al., 2017; Zemoura et al., 2019; Sandberg and Borg, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Inhibition of CaMKII with KN-93 prevented FSS-induced increase in p62/sequestosome-1 protein abundance.
source: In both CaMKII-disrupted cell populations, FSS and PTH failed to increase p62/sequestosome-1 protein abundance (Figure 4G,H)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Expression of dominant negative CaMKII (T286A) prevented PTH-induced increase in p62/sequestosome-1 protein abundance.
source: In both CaMKII-disrupted cell populations, FSS and PTH failed to increase p62/sequestosome-1 protein abundance (Figure 4G,H)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Crinophagy is utilized by peptide-secreting cells to route secretory vesicles to the lysosome rather than being delivered to the membrane for exocytosis.
source: This regulated lysosomal degradation of sclerostin following FSS or PTH treatment is reminiscent of a relatively obscure autophagy pathway known as crinophagy, which is utilized by peptide-secreting cells, such as pancreatic beta-cells, to route secretory vesicles to the lysosome rather than being delivered to the membrane for exocytosis (Lee et al., 2019; Weckman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Crinophagy is regulated by nitric oxide.
source: Interestingly, crinophagy is regulated by nitric oxide (Sandberg and Borg, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Nitric oxide production following mechanical cues is a canonical response in osteocytes.
source: In osteocytes, nitric oxide production following mechanical cues is a canonical response (Klein-Nulend et al., 1998; Zaman et al., 1999; Klein-Nulend et al., 2014; Nagayama et al., 2019; Gohin et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Activation of nitric oxide signaling with SNAP induced a rapid decrease in sclerostin protein in Ocy454 cells.
source: Indeed, activation of nitric oxide signaling in Ocy454 cells with S-Nitroso-N-acetyl-DL-penicillamine (SNAP), a nitric oxide donor, induced a rapid decrease in sclerostin protein (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SNAP-induced rapid reduction of sclerostin protein occurred without increased CaMKII phosphorylation.
source: This rapid reduction of sclerostin protein occurred without increased CaMKII phosphorylation (Figure 5A), suggesting that activation of nitric oxide production may be downstream of CaMKII phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A and represents an inference about pathway order.

claim: Treatment with SNAP in the presence of bafilomycin A1 prevented sclerostin degradation in Ocy454 cells transfected with myc-sclerostin.
source: When Ocy454 cells transfected with myc-sclerostin were treated with SNAP, a nitric oxide donor, in the presence of the lysosome inhibitor bafilomycin A1, sclerostin degradation was prevented (Figure 5B)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Blocking nitric oxide production with L-NAME prevented FSS-activated degradation of sclerostin protein at 5 min.
source: Additionally, blocking nitric oxide production with L-NAME prevented the FSS-activated degradation of sclerostin protein at 5 min, as well as the FSS-induced increase in p62/sequestosome-1 (Figure 5C)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Blocking nitric oxide production with L-NAME prevented FSS-induced increase in p62/sequestosome-1.
source: Additionally, blocking nitric oxide production with L-NAME prevented the FSS-activated degradation of sclerostin protein at 5 min, as well as the FSS-induced increase in p62/sequestosome-1 (Figure 5C)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Hydrogen peroxide or ROS generated by KillerRed were sufficient to activate CaMKII and decrease sclerostin protein abundance.
source: Both hydrogen peroxide (Lyons et al., 2017) or ROS generated by a genetically encoded photoactivatable protein, KillerRed, were sufficient to activate CaMKII and decrease sclerostin protein abundance in Ocy454 and UMR106 cells, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B and a citation to previous work.

claim: Sclerostin protein was rapidly decreased in tibiae treated with hydrogen peroxide ex vivo.
source: Like results found in vitro, sclerostin protein was rapidly decreased in tibiae treated with hydrogen peroxide, supporting a role of ROS in the control of sclerostin abundance in intact bone (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Apocynin pre-treatment blocked load-induced increase in periosteal bone formation rate (Ps.BFR) in mice.
source: Acute administration of apocynin 2 hr prior each bout of ulnar loading blocked the subsequent load-induced increase in periosteal bone formation rate (Ps.BFR) (Figure 6B,C)
evidence: This claim is supported by dynamic histomorphometry data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: Apocynin pre-treatment blocked load-induced increase in mineral apposition rate (Ps.MAR) in mice.
source: and mineral apposition rate (Ps.MAR) (Figure 6B,D)
evidence: This claim is supported by dynamic histomorphometry data shown in Figures 6B and 6D.

claim: Inhibition of NOX2 with apocynin blunted the rapid degradation of sclerostin protein in vivo following ulnar loading.
source: Inhibition of NOX2 with apocynin blunted the rapid degradation of sclerostin protein in vivo (Figure 6E)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Acute administration of bafilomycin A1 prior to ulnar loading reduced the subsequent load-induced increase in Ps.BFR in mice.
source: Acute administration of bafilomycin A1 4 hr prior to each bout of ulnar load reduced the subsequent load-induced increase in Ps.BFR (Figure 7A,B)
evidence: This claim is supported by dynamic histomorphometry data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: Acute administration of bafilomycin A1 prior to ulnar loading reduced the subsequent load-induced increase in Ps.MAR in mice.
source: and Ps.MAR (Figure 7A,C)
evidence: This claim is supported by dynamic histomorphometry data shown in Figures 7A and 7C.

claim: Administration of bafilomycin A1 during the first four days of the experiment had no effect on Ps.BFR or Ps.MAR in the contralateral non-loaded limb.
source: In contrast, the administration of bafilomycin A1 during the first four days of the experiment had no effect on the Ps.BFR or Ps.MAR in the contralateral non-loaded limb.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dynamic histomorphometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inhibition of lysosomal degradation with bafilomycin A1 blunted the rapid degradation of sclerostin protein in vivo following ulnar loading.
source: Inhibition of lysosomal degradation with bafilomycin A1 blunted the rapid degradation of sclerostin protein in vivo (Figure 7D)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Gaucher disease iPSC-derived osteoblasts have significantly increased levels of sclerostin compared to iPSC-derived osteoblasts from healthy patients.
source: Consistent with lysosomal degradation of sclerostin, we observed that iPSC-derived osteoblasts from Gaucher patients had significantly increased levels of sclerostin compared to iPSC-derived osteoblasts from healthy patients without Gaucher disease (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Treating Gaucher iPSC-derived osteoblasts with recombinant GCase restored sclerostin abundance to control levels.
source: Furthermore, treating Gaucher iPSC-derived osteoblasts with recombinant GCase, which restores lysosomal function, β-catenin signaling, and osteoblast differentiation (Panicker et al., 2018), also restored sclerostin abundance to control levels (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7E and a citation to previous work.

claim: Patients with Gaucher disease exhibit skeletal dysplasias and low bone mass.
source: As with many lysosomal storage disorders, patients with Gaucher disease exhibit skeletal dysplasias and low bone mass (Hughes et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Gaucher disease iPSC-derived osteoblasts display defective osteoblast differentiation and mineralization caused by defects in Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
source: Gaucher disease iPSC-derived osteoblasts display defective osteoblast differentiation and mineralization caused by defects in Wnt/β-catenin signaling, an effect that is reversed by treatment with recombinant GCase (Panicker et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Osteocytes respond to distinct osteoanabolic cues (mechanical load and PTH) by redirecting sclerostin from a secretory pathway to the lysosome for rapid degradation.
source: Our data show that osteocytes respond to distinct osteoanabolic cues, mechanical load and PTH, by redirecting sclerostin from a secretory pathway to the lysosome for rapid degradation (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the collective experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In response to mechanical load, sclerostin degradation is mediated by activation of ROS and nitric oxide signaling, a CaMKII-dependent increase in lysosomal activity, and post-translational degradation of sclerostin by the lysosome.
source: In response to mechanical load, this signaling event is mediated by activation of ROS and nitric oxide signaling, a CaMKII-dependent increase in lysosomal activity, and the post-translational degradation of sclerostin by the lysosome.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the collective experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: For PTH, CaMKII is likely a common integrator upstream of lysosomal degradation of sclerostin protein.
source: For PTH, CaMKII is likely a common integrator upstream of lysosomal degradation of sclerostin protein.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by experimental data showing PTH activates CaMKII and that CaMKII inhibition prevents PTH-induced lysosomal activation.

claim: Both lysosomal activity and activation of the upstream mechano-signaling pathway are required for mechanically induced decreases in sclerostin protein and bone formation in vivo.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that both lysosomal activity and activation of the upstream of mechano-signaling pathway are required for mechanically induced decreases in sclerostin protein and bone formation in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the in vivo experiments using apocynin and bafilomycin A1.

claim: Post-translational control of sclerostin may be the first line response to a bone anabolic stimulus, whereas long-term stimulation leads to transcriptional control of the Sost gene.
source: It may be that post-translational control is the first line response to a bone anabolic stimulus, whereas long-term stimulation leads to genome level transcriptional control of the Sost gene.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the integration of the current findings with previous knowledge about transcriptional regulation.

claim: Brief 5 min FSS and short 30 min duration PTH exposure are insufficient to decrease Sost mRNA abundance hours after the stimulus.
source: Indeed, longer periods of loading are required to observe Sost mRNA decreases than are required for loss of protein described here. Our brief, 5 min FSS (Williams et al., 2020) and short, 30 min duration PTH exposure (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) are insufficient to decrease Sost mRNA abundance hours after the stimulus.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and a citation to previous work.

claim: There was no statistical effect of either apocynin or bafilomycin A1 on bone formation rate or mineral apposition rate in the contralateral, non-loaded limb.
source: firstly, there was also no statistical effect of either apocynin or bafilomycin A1 on bone formation rate or mineral apposition rate in the contralateral, non-loaded limb.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dynamic histomorphometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The inhibitors (apocynin and bafilomycin A1) were only present for each bout of ulnar load but were absent during the 7 day bone forming period.
source: Secondly, the inhibitors were only present for each bout of ulnar load but were absent during the 7 day bone forming period, indicating that disruption of the acute downstream response to the mechanical cue, not the ability of the osteoblasts to build bone, caused the reductions in bone formation.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Sclerostin is directed through a Rab27a-positive secretory pathway for exocytosis or is trafficked to the lysosome for degradation, an effect that can be regulated by CaMKII and mechano-activated nitric oxide.
source: Thus, analogous to crinophagy, our data support that sclerostin is directed through a Rab27a-positive secretory pathway for exocytosis or is trafficked to the lysosome for degradation, an effect that can be regulated by CaMKII and mechano-activated nitric oxide.
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating the experimental findings with the crinophagy model.

claim: The increased sclerostin levels observed in Gaucher disease iPSCs are likely to lead to decreased β-catenin activation and osteoblast differentiation.
source: Sclerostin is a canonical Wnt/β-catenin antagonist; therefore, the increased sclerostin levels observed here in Gaucher disease iPSCs are likely to lead to the previously reported decrease in β-catenin activation and osteoblast differentiation (Panicker et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of sclerostin and the observed increase in sclerostin in Gaucher disease cells.

claim: Restoring expression of glucocerebrosidase in Gaucher disease iPSCs lowers sclerostin abundance, which could explain the rescue in β-catenin activation and osteoblast differentiation.
source: Likewise, we showed that restoring expression of the missing hydrolase, glucocerebrosidase, in Gaucher disease iPSCs lowers sclerostin abundance, which could explain the rescue in β-catenin activation and osteoblast differentiation reported previously (Panicker et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing rGCase treatment lowers sclerostin and previous work showing rGCase rescues β-catenin signaling.

claim: Lysosome activity is diminished with age.
source: Lysosome activity is diminished with age (Moore, 2020; Stead et al., 2019), including in the osteocyte during age-related bone loss (Chen et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Diminished lysosome activity with age could impair sclerostin degradation and new bone formation even in the face of osteoanabolic signals.
source: an effect that could impair sclerostin degradation and new bone formation even in the face of osteoanabolic signals.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the integration of the current findings with knowledge about aging.

claim: Targeting autophagy and lysosome activity to improve bone mass in aging has been proposed.
source: While undoubtedly multifaceted in its impacts, targeting autophagy and lysosome activity to improve bone mass in aging has been proposed (Li et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Impacts on sclerostin bioavailability might contribute mechanistically to the efficacy of targeting autophagy and lysosome activity to improve bone mass in aging.
source: and these data suggest that impacts on sclerostin bioavailability might contribute mechanistically to its efficacy.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the integration of the current findings with proposed therapeutic approaches.

claim: Targeting sclerostin may be important to interventions to improve bone mass in lysosomal storage disorders, like Gaucher disease.
source: Additionally, targeting sclerostin may be important to interventions to improve bone mass in lysosomal storage disorders, like Gaucher disease.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the findings in Gaucher disease iPSCs.

claim: Sclerostin co-localizes with lysosomes, but not all sclerostin is contained in lysosomes and not all lysosomes contain sclerostin.
source: In 3D projections of Z-stacks, it is clear that sclerostin co-localizes with lysosomes identified by siR-lysosome, but not all sclerostin is contained in lysosomes and not all lysosomes contain sclerostin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D imaging analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mechano-activated nitric oxide production is downstream of CaMKII phosphorylation.
source: This rapid reduction of sclerostin protein occurred without increased CaMKII phosphorylation (Figure 5A), suggesting that activation of nitric oxide production may be downstream of CaMKII phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that SNAP (nitric oxide donor) decreases sclerostin without activating CaMKII.

claim: Nitric oxide is sufficient to drive the lysosomal degradation of sclerostin.
source: When Ocy454 cells transfected with myc-sclerostin were treated with SNAP, a nitric oxide donor, in the presence of the lysosome inhibitor bafilomycin A1, sclerostin degradation was prevented (Figure 5B), confirming that nitric oxide is sufficient to drive the lysosomal degradation of sclerostin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing SNAP decreases sclerostin and this is prevented by lysosome inhibition.

claim: Nitric oxide is necessary for FSS-activated degradation of sclerostin protein.
source: Additionally, blocking nitric oxide production with L-NAME prevented the FSS-activated degradation of sclerostin protein at 5 min, as well as the FSS-induced increase in p62/sequestosome-1 (Figure 5C), supporting a role of nitric oxide in the activation of the lysosome and degradation of sclerostin, likely upstream of the lysosome and downstream of CaMKII.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing L-NAME prevents FSS-induced sclerostin degradation.

claim: Nitric oxide acts upstream of the lysosome and downstream of CaMKII in the mechano-transduction pathway.
source: Additionally, blocking nitric oxide production with L-NAME prevented the FSS-activated degradation of sclerostin protein at 5 min, as well as the FSS-induced increase in p62/sequestosome-1 (Figure 5C), supporting a role of nitric oxide in the activation of the lysosome and degradation of sclerostin, likely upstream of the lysosome and downstream of CaMKII.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing the effects of L-NAME and SNAP.

claim: NOX2-derived ROS is necessary for sclerostin degradation in vivo.
source: Inhibition of NOX2 with apocynin blunted the rapid degradation of sclerostin protein in vivo (Figure 6E), supporting that NOX2 ROS is necessary for sclerostin degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo data showing apocynin prevents load-induced sclerostin degradation.

claim: Lysosomal function is necessary for the rapid degradation of sclerostin in vivo.
source: Inhibition of lysosomal degradation with bafilomycin A1 blunted the rapid degradation of sclerostin protein in vivo (Figure 7D), supporting that lysosomal function is necessary for the rapid degradation of sclerostin.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo data showing bafilomycin A1 prevents load-induced sclerostin degradation.
